title: Rewrite BotTools, TrumpBot and Support
issueTitle: Phase 0 · 7 — Rewrite BotTools and the private repositories, and replace the private repository clone
function: BotTools, which is public, and TrumpBot and Support, which are private, still hold in their histories the files the phase purges: 39 purged blobs in BotTools, all of them also reachable through its pull-request refs, 199 in TrumpBot and 7,259 in Support. The local TrumpBot clone still holds TrumpBot's old history. The unit takes each repository through the rewrite pipeline as GKB2 and GKB were taken, BotTools first, then TrumpBot, then Support: the purge with its checks before and after, the force-push with its per-ref verification, the exit tests on a fresh mirror and the residual probes, with BotTools' pull-request residual counted. Once TrumpBot's push is proven, the clone is replaced by a fresh one at the same path, its four untracked files kept. The unit spans four systems, the toolchain, the rewrite pipeline, the residual-exposure measurement and the clone realignment, so this run designs it and splits it into units; nothing is rewritten, pushed or replaced in this run. Unit 7 of #2, with no version moved; the three repositories keep their visibility.

wip.detail: Document: 3 of 3 tasks done; every task done.

interview.text: Should each part of the unit stay inside one of the registry's systems, or may a rewrite part also extend the tools it runs and measure its own repository's residual, as the GKB2 and GKB unit did?
options: Size them as the GKB2 and GKB unit was sized: each rewrite runs stages 1 to 9 for its repository and extends the tools it needs; only the clone replacement stands apart

One registry system each: the tool work is its own part with no GitHub write, the rewrites stop at stage 8, one residual part probes all three repositories after the last push, and the clone replacement is its own part
interview.answer: Each part stays inside one system: the tools part extends the workspace tools before any push, with no write to GitHub; the rewrites run stages 1 to 8 for each repository, with BotTools' pull-request residual counted on its fresh mirror; one residual measurement runs stage 9 over all three repositories once the last push is verified; and the clone replacement is its own part, once TrumpBot's push is proven.

interview.text: What of the old TrumpBot clone's local state should the fresh clone keep? Besides the four files under .idea/ the clone now holds a knowledge graph built from the pre-rewrite tree, its exclude entry, two graph hooks and two local config keys.
options: Keep everything: archive and restore the graph files, the exclude entry, the hooks and the two config keys
Keep the four .idea/ files only; the clone ends with no graph and no graph hooks
Keep the four .idea/ files only, and rebuild the graph from the rewritten tree once the fresh clone is proven
interview.answer: The fresh clone keeps the four `.idea/` files only; once it is proven, the graph is rebuilt from the rewritten tree by a code-only build, which installs the two hooks again.

interview.text: Should BotTools' dormant CircleCI webhook stay as it is while its two branches are force-pushed?
options: Leave it; the deliveries are recorded by count with the push
Deactivate it before the push and reactivate it after
interview.answer: The webhook stays as it is, and the deliveries the push makes are recorded by count.

architecture.detail: Unit 7 of the history rewrite: BotTools, TrumpBot and Support are rewritten and force-pushed as GKB2 and GKB were, BotTools' pull-request residual is measured, and the local TrumpBot clone is replaced. The unit touches three systems, so this run designs it and splits it into units; nothing is built or pushed in this run. Next: the design, starting with the questions on intent.

Research complete: 31 of the 32 claims hold at source and the one that fails was a wrong file citation for behaviour that holds. Each repository is pushed in one request as one atomic push with an explicit lease on every branch, after a dry run. The old TrumpBot clone is moved aside by a rename on its own volume and deleted last. The tools are rebuilt in a new folder, and the earlier folder stays as it ran. Next: the grand design and its units.

research.detail: The 32 outside-world claims the three findings rest on are being checked at their sources.

tasks.report: The four planning documents are committed at d5192fc; main had not moved, so there was nothing to merge, and no version moved. The design and its consequences are final: the design leaves no consideration open, and what the units leave behind is recorded as known gaps and follow-ups in the consequences. Next: the state boards, with the four planned units drawn dashed.

milestones.label: Research verified
milestones.note: three questions, each with its findings file; 31 of the 32 load-bearing claims hold at their sources, and the one that fails is a wrong file citation for behaviour that holds, so no recommendation changes. Each repository's branches go in one atomic push with an explicit lease on every branch, after a dry run of the same line, and a read-back of every branch names the server's state after any failure; the old TrumpBot clone is moved aside by one rename on its own volume, the fresh clone keeps the four `.idea/` files and the old clone is deleted last; the tools are rebuilt in a new folder, the earlier folder kept as it ran, with every recorded gap closed before the first push and four further gaps found that would stop a run. Where the sources disagreed, BotTools' webhook deliveries are counted once, right after its push, and the residual measurement follows the last push promptly

verdict.defense: One procedure serves the three repositories, each stopping on its own gates with its own state, so three units would repeat it and move the residual measurement further from BotTools' push. Push protection refuses BotTools' push: the remote is unchanged, the two private repositories wait, and the unit never bypasses it
A reply is misread: it is stored as delivered, the classifier stops on what it cannot read, and the server's state is read from GitHub whatever the reply says
BotTools' deliveries leave GitHub's three-day list: they are counted at stage 7, right after the push

options.name: The old clone renamed aside on its own volume, a fresh clone at the same path with the four `.idea/` files restored, the old clone deleted after the fresh one is read back, then the graph rebuilt from the rewritten tree
options.why: The rename is the lock probe and widens access by nobody, the replacement and the deletion are two procedures with the read-back between them, and the graph describes the rewritten tree.

options.name: The clone replacement as the last step of the rewrites
options.why: A stop in the replacement would hold the rewrites' landing and the residual measurement, although neither depends on the clone, and its write is to a checkout, not to GitHub.

options.name: Moving the old clone into the workspace
options.why: The workspace is on another volume, so the move is a copy followed by a deletion: no lock probe, a mostly deleted source when a file is held, and the irreversible step first.

options.name: A restricted folder on the clone's volume for the old clone
options.why: A renamed tree keeps its own access entries, and every account may traverse a folder it cannot list, so the folder narrows nothing and adds a folder to remove.

options.name: Leaving the old clone's deletion to the workspace's deletion
options.why: The old clone is outside the workspace, so that deletion never reaches it, and the pre-rewrite objects would outlive this work on the clone's volume.

options.name: Carrying the old clone's graph into the fresh clone

options.name: The graph build before the old clone's deletion
options.why: The old clone is no fallback for the build, so waiting for it would only keep the pre-rewrite objects outside the workspace for longer.

options.name: The replacement and the deletion as one procedure
options.why: The unit's own read of the fresh clone would come after the irreversible step; two procedures put that read between them.

excerpt.heading: 10.2 The move
excerpt.paragraph: Where. The old clone is moved aside by one rename on its own volume: `%PROJECTS%\TrumpBot` becomes `%PROJECTS%\TrumpBot-old`. A move into the workspace would cross volumes, and that is a copy followed by a deletion: no lock probe, and the irreversible step first. · Guards before it: the target is absent; the clone and the target's parent are on the same volume, compared by `stat -c %d`, so that `mv` can never copy; the count of open files is 0; no …

excerpt.paragraph: Carried: the four `.idea/` files, archived with a checksum list behind a closed-set guard over the 59 files git does not track: 4 under `.idea/`, 55 under `graphify-out/`, 0 anywhere else. A file outside the two folders is a stop, because it would be dropped silently. The carried folder and the not-carried folder are policy values. · Not carried: the 55 graph files, the exclude entry, the two hooks and the two extra configuration keys. The graph was built from the pre-rewrite tree, so it describes files the rewrite removes. The hooks and the exclude entry are recorded by name, size and …

The restored set must equal the four-file list byte for byte, with every checksum matching. · The proofs, made by the procedure and again by the unit before it requests the deletion: · the remote-tracking refs equal `ref-map`'s new column, and `main` equals its remote-tracking branch; · one pack, no loose object, a clean `fsck`; · every pre-rewrite commit of TrumpBot and every manifest blob is missing from the clone; · …

excerpt.paragraph: Unit 4, `clone-replacement`. It runs once TrumpBot's push is proven: TrumpBot holds its stage-8 marker, and the server's heads equal `ref-map`'s new column.

verdict.defense: A rename on the clone's own volume refuses with no effect while anything inside is open and keeps the tree's access entries, while a move into the workspace would cross volumes: a copy, then a deletion, with the irreversible step first. The graph describes files the rewrite removes, so it is rebuilt rather than carried. The deletion waits for the unit's read of the fresh clone and not for the graph build, so the pre-rewrite objects stay outside the workspace no longer than the replacement needs.
tests: The self-test's quick gate, run again by the unit
risks: Between the move and the deletion the old clone holds every pre-rewrite object of TrumpBot beside the clone, no wider than today's clone; the deletion follows the read-back and does not wait for the graph
A process holds a file inside the clone: the rename refuses and changes nothing, and a bounded retry outlasts a scanner
A cross-volume move by accident: the same-volume and absent-target guards come before the rename, and the outcome is read from the two paths
The fresh clone carries more or less than intended: the closed-set guard over the 59 files, the restored set compared with the four-file list, and the exact-set proofs of keys, hooks and excludes
The graph build does not run, or leaves another footprint: the replacement stands without it, and the read-back records what it left

impact.summary: No module is published and no version moves: every landing of #27 and its units carries documents and generated boards only. BotTools, which is public, and TrumpBot and Support, which are private, are force-pushed in place, one atomic push each: every commit id changes, the purged files leave every commit, and each keeps its visibility and default branch. BotTools' pull-request refs keep its 39 purged blobs fetchable, and the TrumpBot clone on this machine is replaced by a fresh one.

release.note: a tracking plan moves no version, and no unit publishes a module

downstream.summary: Every commit id changes, as every root commit holds a purged path: BotTools' 16 commits become 15, TrumpBot's 11 become 9 and Support's 2 become 1. The files under the purged paths leave every commit, the tips' trees included, and every branch changes: BotTools' and TrumpBot's two and Support's one. No issue, pull request, comment, label, setting or webhook is changed, and nothing is deleted.

GitHub keeps serving every pre-rewrite object by id. BotTools' pull-request refs keep 13 old commits and all 39 purged blobs fetchable, and its two pull requests keep showing their pre-rewrite commits; BotTools was public before, so this exposure is not new. TrumpBot's and Support's old objects stay readable to signed-in readers with access, and to nobody anonymously.

Each rewritten branch adds one force-push entry to its repository's activity feed, whose `before` is a pre-rewrite tip, and one event. BotTools' webhook, to a CircleCI host, receives one push delivery per branch, 2 in all, recorded by count; it stays as it is.

They keep the old histories, and their branches share no commit with the server's afterwards. None of the three repositories has a fork, and the one known clone on this machine, TrumpBot's, is replaced.

Replaced by a fresh clone at the same path that keeps its four `.idea/` files. The old code knowledge graph, built from the pre-rewrite tree, goes with the old clone, with its exclude entry, its two hooks and two extra configuration keys; a code-only graph of the rewritten tree is built afterwards. Until its deletion the old clone sits beside it on the same volume, outside the workspace, holding TrumpBot's pre-rewrite objects.

downstream.who: The workspace and the data folder
downstream.summary: A second tool folder beside the GKB2 and GKB unit's, which stays as it ran; the three mirrors rewritten beside their untouched backups, a fresh mirror of each, and each repository's records and report row in the data folder. They hold pre-rewrite ids and paths and are never committed.

The phase design and the phase consequences take 20 and 5 dated notes with this design's landing, the GKB2 and GKB unit's consequences one per gap and follow-up the tools unit closes, and the registry of systems the four units in place of unit 7. No legacy repository receives a commit.

adaptation.summary: For these three repositories, every branch goes in one atomic push with an explicit lease on its recorded tip, after a dry run, and after every non-zero status a read-back of every branch names the state: neither, both or partial. The GKB2 and GKB unit's one-branch push is its case of one branch.
For these three repositories it runs as its own unit after the last push, within the events' window, not right after each push.

A clone is moved aside by a rename on its own volume, guarded to stay on that volume, its outcome read from whether each of the two paths exists. This replaces a move into the workspace, which on this machine crosses volumes.

The GKB2 and GKB unit's folder is kept as it ran and never saved again, the preparation unit's clone scripts are replaced by the clone set and never run, and the two workspace scripts that pin the earlier scan configuration stay unrun. A further repository is a row of the parameter table.

Stays blocked by #27, and takes the three report rows with BotTools' pull-request residual and webhook delivery count, the residual records, every unit's records with their checksum lists, any default-rule finding by rule id and count, both tool folders and the stage runner to copy, and the record that no old-clone path remains, whose path its cleanup confirms absent.
